topic: The Fake Video Call That Stole $400 Million
title: THE FAKE VIDEO CALL
THAT STOLE $400 MILLION

script.text: This is your friend, on a video call. Except they're not really there. It's a recording. And the FBI says North Korean hackers have used this trick to steal more than four hundred million dollars in crypto. Here's the twist. It's usually not an AI deepfake. It's real webcam video, secretly recorded from a previous victim. The FBI calls it FaceStealer.

It starts with someone who's already been hacked. Call them Victim A. The hackers have scanned their computer for crypto wallets, taken over their Telegram account, and while Victim A waited for a video chat to start, secretly recorded their webcam. Now the hackers become Victim A. They message Victim A's contacts from the real account. Let's catch up. Let's discuss collaboration. They can even read the chat history, so messages to high-value targets are tailored to past conversations.

Say yes, and a calendar invite arrives, with no meeting link. The link only comes shortly before the call. It looks like Zoom or Teams, but it's a look-alike address the hackers registered, leading to a copycat meeting room. You wait in the lobby. You're admitted. And the hackers press play on Victim A's recorded webcam video, often with extra videos, so the room seems full of people you know.

After a short delay, your friend sends a message. There's an audio problem. Nobody can hear you. The other participants add pressure. So your friend walks you through the fix. Click an update. Run a script. Or paste code into your terminal. That's the infection. The malware installs a cookie harvester, keyloggers, screen capturers, and a backdoor. And from the moment you clicked that first link, they were recording your webcam too. Now you're the next Victim A. With every victim, the FBI says, the pool of targets grows exponentially.

The hackers are patient. In several cases, the theft came months, even more than a year later, as they waited for wallet balances to grow. Under a federal warrant, the FBI seized more than nine hundred of these webcam videos. So where does AI fit in? The FBI says the hackers have begun using what it calls super intelligence to deepfake well-known people in crypto. But the scheme still overwhelmingly relies on genuine, stolen video. No deepfake needed. A real face was enough.

It gets worse. Earlier this year, the hackers used the same trick on the maintainer of a major open-source JavaScript library. A fake Teams call, with several participants, including someone he recognized. He followed the fix. The hackers then used his access to create malicious dependencies, for a library downloaded tens of millions of times a week. The FBI says that without quick detection, it could easily have hit victims on a very large scale. The FBI attributes FaceStealer to North Korean state-sponsored hackers, known publicly as Sapphire Sleet, BlueNoroff, and A.P.T. 38, among other names.

So how do you protect yourself? Here's what the FBI advises. Join with the official app and an invite code, not a link. Keep your webcam off until you can see and hear the person who invited you. Never run a script or paste code to fix a meeting. Confirm the call through a different channel. And secure your chat apps with multi-factor authentication. If you think you've been hit, move your crypto to a new wallet on a clean device, warn your contacts, and report it at I.C.3 dot gov, with the keyword FaceStealer.

A familiar face on a screen is no longer proof. Before you join, ask yourself: is this person really here? Subscribe for more scam breakdowns, and send this to someone who needs it. Because the next call might not be a friend.

science.claim: FaceStealer has stolen more than $400 million in cryptocurrency over the past 18 months, per the FBI; the FBI seized over 900 victim webcam videos.
science.working: Quoted from the FBI FLASH summary: 'stolen more than $400 million in cryptocurrency over the past 18 months'; 'identified and seized over 900 victim webcam videos'. The DOJ release says the same ('more than $400 million', 'over 900 webcam videos').
science.source: FBI FLASH AC-111226-MS (12 Nov 2026), ic3.gov/CSA/2026/261112.pdf; DOJ press release 26-1356 (12 Nov 2026)

science.claim: Attack chain: hijacked account invites target, calendar invite, typo-squatted fake Zoom/Teams link, prerecorded victim webcam video plays, fake audio error, 'fix' (update prompt, script, or pasted terminal code) installs malware, target becomes next victim.
science.working: FBI FLASH Stages 1 to 6, paraphrased. Malware named: browser cookie harvester, keyloggers, screen capturers, backdoor. The webcam recording starts when the imposter link is first clicked.

science.claim: Deepfakes are emerging, but the scheme still overwhelmingly relies on genuine stolen victim video.
science.working: FBI FLASH 'Emerging Use of SI to Generate Deepfake Videos': hackers use 'super intelligence (SI)' to make deepfakes of well-known crypto/web3 figures from public photos; 'the FaceStealer scheme currently continues to overwhelmingly rely on the theft of genuine victim videos'.

science.claim: Theft sometimes came months to over a year after the compromise; hackers copy seed phrases and wait for balances to grow.
science.working: FBI FLASH: 'months to over a year after the initial compromise as the hackers waited for the balances ... to increase'; 'copy recovery phrases, patiently monitor balances ... and reconstitute the wallet'.

science.claim: A major open-source JavaScript library (tens of millions of downloads per week) was nearly compromised; quick detection prevented large-scale victimisation.
science.working: FBI FLASH 'Targeting Open-Source Software Developers': maintainer lured into a fake Teams chat; hackers created malicious dependencies; 'The library receives tens of millions of downloads per week. If not for the quick detection and response ... could easily have resulted in very large-scale victimization.' Library is not named by the FBI.

science.claim: FBI attributes it to North Korean state-sponsored hackers (Sapphire Sleet, UNC1069, Dangerous Password, CryptoCore, APT38, BlueNoroff, Stardust Chollima).
science.working: Names listed verbatim in the FLASH and in the DOJ release.

science.claim: FBI recommendations: official app and invite code; webcam off until you can see and hear the inviter; never run scripts or paste code to update; confirm via another channel; MFA and login alerts on messaging apps; large balances on a physical ledger and no seed phrases on devices. If compromised: new wallet on a clean device, warn contacts, report at IC3.gov with keyword FaceStealer.
science.working: FBI FLASH Recommendations and 'What You Should Do If You Suspect You Have Been Compromised'.
